guideTitle: 6 Best Measuring Cups and Spoons Sets in 2026
metaTitle: Best Measuring Cups and Spoons Sets (2026)
metaDescription: Six combined measuring cups and spoons sets compared on size range, metric markings, handle comfort and storage, from steel starter kits to colored plastic.
introParagraphs: Buying cups and spoons as a matched set sounds like the easy route, and it can be, but sets differ widely in what they actually hold. One box may stop at four cups and five spoons, while another contains seven cups, seven spoons, tiny spice scoops and a leveler. If you are furnishing a first kitchen, replacing a drawer of mismatched plastic or buying for a relative who just moved, the contents list matters more than the brand name.

The six sets here run from lean to loaded. The TILUCK with silicone handles and the AskBed offer ten pieces each, one in 18/8 steel and one in light plastic. The HAWOWZ is a colored twelve-piece plastic set. The THLHKD 16-piece adds milliliter-sized spoons, the EWFEN stacks seven cups, seven spoons and five mini spoons, and the Spring Chef packs fourteen pieces plus a leveler into a single-piece steel build.

We evaluated each set from its listing specifications and common buyer feedback themes, so sizes, materials and counts are as the maker states them. We left out prices, ratings and review counts. Where a detail is unclear in the listing, we say so rather than guess.

products.name: Spring Chef 14 Piece Stainless Steel Measuring Cups and Spoons with Leveler
products.description:
The Spring Chef is the most complete combined set here. The listing names seven cups running 1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4 and 1 cup with a pour spout, six spoons at 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 1 teaspoon plus 1 tablespoon, a leveler and a ring. That makes it the only set in this group that includes a 3/4 teaspoon spoon, a size many recipes for spice blends and baking powder use.

The maker also describes single-piece metal construction with a wide, long handle. A one-piece build means no rivets or welded joints where moisture and flour can collect, and no handle that can twist loose over the years. The wide handle is a comfort feature, particularly for people who find thin steel handles hard on the fingers, and the pour spout on the cups helps when you scoop from a bag and tip into a bowl.

The tradeoff is bulk. Fourteen pieces on rings is a lot to keep in one drawer, and you will occasionally untangle the stack to find the 2/3 cup. Compared with the TILUCK silicone-handle set, which has five cups and five spoons, the Spring Chef covers every odd size and adds the leveler, which makes sloppy heaped spoons easier to avoid. If you want a set that handles any recipe and never runs short of the right size, this is the one to buy.
products.bestFor: Bakers and serious home cooks who want every odd size plus a leveler in one set.
pros: Leveler and ring in the box
Single piece steel has no weak joints
cons: Ring bundle needs untangling for one size

products.name: EWFEN 7 Cup and 7 Spoon Stainless Steel Set with Mini Spoons
products.description:
The EWFEN is a loaded steel set: seven nesting cups from 1/8 to 1 cup, seven spoons and five mini spoons, with further items referenced in the listing. The maker says each cup and spoon is made from a single piece of metal so the handles will never bend or break. It also notes outside markings that show a smaller measurement visible on the inside, which is a feature designed to help you read the size while the cup is full.

The five mini spoons are the real differentiator for anyone who cooks with spices. A pinch-sized scoop for cloves or cayenne, kept apart from the larger spoons, spares you from eyeballing tiny amounts. The set is also unusually complete on cup sizes, including 2/3 and 3/4, which makes it a solid fit for baking from older family recipes where those measures turn up often.

Compared with the Spring Chef, the EWFEN has more total pieces but no mention of a 3/4 teaspoon spoon in the listing text provided, so check the full size list before buying if you use that measure. Compared with the TILUCK, it is a much larger kit. The cost of that completeness is storage, since a dozen-plus separate pieces need a deep drawer or a hook. Choose it if you cook spice-forward dishes and want the whole range of small measures.
products.bestFor: Spice-heavy cooks who want tiny scoops and every cup size in one steel kit.
pros: Five mini spoons for pinch amounts
cons: A large set needs deep drawer space
Mini spoons are easy to misplace

products.name: TILUCK Nesting Cups and Spoons Set with Silicone Handles
products.description:
This TILUCK variant swaps the bare steel handle for a soft silicone one. The listing names five cups at 1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 and 1 cup, five spoons from 1/4 teaspoon to 1 tablespoon, food-grade 18/8 stainless steel, and a heavy-duty, dishwasher-safe design. The silicone grip is the main upgrade over the more basic all-steel TILUCK sets.

A cushioned handle matters for comfort. Steel handles can feel cold, slick and narrow in a wet hand, and a soft grip gives you a firmer hold when you scoop sticky honey or tap a cup against a bowl. For anyone who finds thin metal uncomfortable, silicone provides a gentler contact surface, and it also cuts noise when the pieces knock against one another in the drawer.

The set has gaps that the Spring Chef and EWFEN fill. There is no 2/3 or 3/4 cup, and no 1/8 teaspoon spoon in the list, so a recipe calling for those sizes means two scoops. If you only bake a few times a month, those omissions will rarely bite. If you want a tidy ten-piece set with a friendly grip and a steel build, and you want something simpler than the larger kits, the silicone-handle TILUCK is the comfortable middle choice.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prioritize a cushioned grip and a compact ten piece steel set.
cons: No 1/8 teaspoon spoon in the list

products.name: THLHKD 16 Piece Measuring Cups and Spoons Set with Metric Markings
specs: Spoons in tsp, tbsp and ml
products.description:
The THLHKD 16-piece set is built for cooks who work in both US and metric. The listing names cups from 1/8 to 1 cup, spoons in teaspoon and tablespoon sizes, and a separate row of spoons marked 30, 20, 15, 10 and 5 milliliters. Each piece is said to be clearly engraved with both US and metric measurements, so you can follow a European recipe or a US one without a conversion chart.

Engraved markings are worth paying attention to. Printed marks fade in the dishwasher, but engraved ones stay legible, and a set with two systems on the same handle saves arithmetic mid-recipe. The milliliter spoons are especially useful for medicine-style dosing of liquid flavorings, oils and extracts, where a tablespoon is a loose approximation. They also suit anyone who bakes from metric recipes and scales by weight.

The set lacks a 2/3 or 3/4 cup in the list, and it is a lot of small pieces to manage. Compared with the Spring Chef, it has two extra metric spoon sizes but fewer cup sizes. Compared with the AskBed, it uses a metal build rather than plastic. It is an excellent fit for households that use metric recipes, international cookbooks or a mix of both, and a less natural fit for someone who only ever needs US cup sizes.
products.bestFor: Cooks who follow both metric and US recipes and want engraved dual markings.
cons: Sixteen pieces are fiddly to store

products.name: AskBed 10 Piece Measuring Cups and Spoons Set with Non Slip Handles
products.description:
The AskBed is a ten-piece plastic set with five cups and five spoons: spoons from 1/4 teaspoon to 1 tablespoon and cups beginning at 1/8 cup. The listing says the markings are engraved with relief fonts in both metric and standard units, the material is BPA-free high-grade PP plastic, and the handles are non-slip. It is the light, no-fuss way to get a complete set.

Raised markings are a useful accessibility touch, because they can be read by feel as well as by sight, which helps in a dim kitchen or when your reading glasses are on the other side of the room. The non-slip handles help with wet hands, and plastic will not clang or scratch a nonstick pan. The listing calls the cups heat and cold resistant, which means they handle warm liquids and fridge items.

Plastic is less rigid than steel, so the rims can deform with years of use and the cups can stain from tomato sauce or turmeric. The set also omits the 2/3 and 3/4 cup sizes. Compared with the Spring Chef or TILUCK, it is a lighter-duty option; compared with the HAWOWZ, it offers fewer cup sizes. It suits a first apartment, a vacation rental kitchen, or someone who wants a light, quiet set without any metal.
products.bestFor: Light-duty everyday use, rentals and anyone who prefers a quiet plastic set.
pros: Raised markings can be read by touch
Non slip handles for wet hands
cons: Plastic can stain and soften over time

products.name: HAWOWZ 12 Piece Colored Measuring Cups and Spoons Set
products.description:
The HAWOWZ is a twelve-piece set with six cups and matching spoons, and the listing explicitly names the cup sizes: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 2/3 and 3/4 cup. The pieces are colored and nest for storage. This is the only plastic set in the group that includes both 2/3 and 3/4 cup, which gives it a full-range cup lineup at the plastic tier.

Color coding is a practical feature. Each size has its own hue, so you can reach for the 'blue' cup without reading the number, and a child or a helper in the kitchen can follow a recipe by color. It also makes it easy to spot a missing piece when you wash up. The bright colors suit a family kitchen where several people cook, and the pieces nest to keep the drawer tidy.

The listing excerpt available is brief, so confirm the spoon sizes and the material details on the product page before you buy. Compared with the AskBed, the HAWOWZ gives you a fuller cup range but not the raised markings. Compared with the steel Spring Chef, it is lighter and gentler on the hand but less rigid and less likely to last for decades. It fits a household that values color coding and a complete cup lineup at a modest level.
products.bestFor: Family kitchens that like color coding and want 2/3 and 3/4 cup in a light set.
cons: Plastic is less rigid than steel

buyingCriteria.criterion: What the contents list really includes
buyingCriteria.explanation: Piece counts mislead. Ten pieces can mean five cups and five spoons, as on the AskBed, or it can mean four cups and six spoons. The Spring Chef reaches fourteen pieces by adding a leveler and a ring, while the EWFEN gets there with five mini spoons. Count cups and spoons separately and compare the size lists to the recipes you cook. A longer list is only better if it fills the gaps you actually have, such as 2/3 cup or 3/4 teaspoon.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Odd sizes that recipes quietly demand
buyingCriteria.explanation: The 1/8 teaspoon, 3/4 teaspoon, 2/3 cup and 3/4 cup are the sizes that sets most often drop. The Spring Chef and EWFEN include 2/3 and 3/4 cup, the HAWOWZ includes them in plastic, and the TILUCK and AskBed leave them out. When a size is missing you have to scoop twice, which compounds rounding error. If you bake or follow older cookbooks, favor a set with the odd sizes.

More recipes are written in grams and milliliters now, and a set with dual markings saves a conversion step. The THLHKD 16-piece engraves both systems and adds milliliter spoons from 5 to 30, and the AskBed carries metric and standard in raised relief. Look for engraved or stamped markings rather than printed ones, which fade in the dishwasher. Dual labeling matters most if you use online recipes from different countries.

You will hold these tools every time you cook, so the handle matters. The TILUCK silicone-handle set gives a soft, secure grip, the Spring Chef offers a wide, long steel handle, and the AskBed uses non-slip plastic. Thin steel handles can dig into the hand and slip when wet. If you have tired hands, favor soft or wide handles, and test whether you can hold the cup level with one hand.

Stainless steel sets like the Spring Chef, EWFEN and TILUCK last longest and resist stains, while plastic sets like the AskBed and HAWOWZ are lighter and quieter but can warp or stain. One-piece steel construction, as on the Spring Chef and EWFEN, avoids joints that can loosen. Check that the rim of a plastic cup stays flat after a hot wash, since a warped rim no longer levels accurately. If you plan to keep a set for many years, steel is the better investment.

A large set is a clutter problem if it is not organized. Rings keep pieces together but slow access, nesting saves space, and color coding helps you find a size fast. The HAWOWZ uses nesting colors, the Spring Chef bundles on rings with a leveler, and the EWFEN's mini spoons need their own spot. Think about your drawer depth and pick a set whose total size fits it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the cup and spoon size lists against the amounts that recipes call for. The Spring Chef and EWFEN lead with seven cups each, the HAWOWZ covers six, and the TILUCK silicone set and AskBed stop at five. We also noted whether a set includes the 3/4 teaspoon and 1/8 teaspoon spoons, which many sets omit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Markings and readability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how each set labels its sizes. The THLHKD engraves US and metric units, the AskBed uses raised relief fonts, and the EWFEN adds outside markings that show a smaller measurement. We favored engraved or raised marks over printed ones because they last through dishwasher cycles and can be read by touch.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material and construction
howWeEvaluated.description: Steel was scored for durability and plastic for lightness. The one-piece builds on the Spring Chef and EWFEN scored highest for long life, the TILUCK 18/8 steel followed, and the plastic AskBed and HAWOWZ were rated as lighter-duty. We relied on the maker's stated materials, and we did not claim hands-on durability testing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Comfort and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed handle shape, grip texture and weight. The silicone handle on the TILUCK is the most cushioned, the Spring Chef's wide handle helps with leverage, and the AskBed's non-slip handles help with wet hands. Sets with many small pieces were marked down slightly for handling effort.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The Spring Chef leads on completeness, the EWFEN on small spice scoops, the THLHKD on metric support, the TILUCK on grip comfort, the AskBed on touch-readable markings and the HAWOWZ on color coding. Badges follow these differences, and we avoided any prices, ratings or review counts.

cards.label: Stainless steel
cards.text: Steel is rigid, so rims stay flat for leveling, and it resists stains and odors. The Spring Chef, EWFEN, TILUCK and THLHKD fall on this side. The downside is that steel handles can feel thin or slick, and a set with many pieces can clatter. Choose steel if you plan to keep the set for many years or bake often.

cards.text: Plastic is light, quiet and gentle on cookware, and it does not get hot. The AskBed and HAWOWZ are the plastic picks here. The downside is that it can stain from tomato or turmeric and may warp in high heat. Choose plastic if weight or noise matter, or for a second set in a vacation kitchen.

faq.q: Which sizes should a good cups and spoons set include?
faq.a: A well-rounded set has cups at 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4 and 1, with 1/8 as a bonus, and spoons at 1/4, 1/2 and 1 teaspoon plus 1/2 and 1 tablespoon. The 1/8 and 3/4 teaspoon sizes are the ones most often missing. The Spring Chef and EWFEN come closest to this list. If your set lacks a size, you can combine others, but accuracy drops with each extra scoop.

They are if you cook with spices or flavorings in small quantities. The EWFEN includes five mini spoons designed for pinch-sized amounts, and the THLHKD 13-piece variant adds two. Standard spoons are fine for most baking, but a 1/8 teaspoon size helps with cayenne, cloves and salt. If you rarely measure that small, you can skip them.

faq.q: How do I keep a big set organized?
faq.a: Use the ring that comes with the set, store the ring on a hook inside a cabinet door, and keep mini spoons on their own small ring. Nesting sets like the HAWOWZ stack inside each other. A shallow drawer divider also keeps spoons from tangling. If you find yourself untangling the same ring daily, split the set in two.

faq.q: Can I use the same spoon for dry and wet ingredients?
faq.a: Yes, spoons are generally used for both. Level dry ingredients across the top, and fill wet ingredients until the surface is just level. Do not use a heaped spoon unless the recipe says so. A leveler, like the one in the Spring Chef set, makes dry measuring more consistent.

faq.q: Do metric markings matter for a US kitchen?
faq.a: They matter if you use recipes from other countries or follow online baking blogs, where milliliters and grams are common. Dual markings, like those on the THLHKD, let you switch without a chart. If you only follow US cookbooks, they are a nice extra rather than a need. Engraved marks last longer than printed ones.

faq.q: How long should a measuring set last?
faq.a: A stainless steel set can last for decades if it is not bent or dropped, since steel does not stain or absorb odors. Plastic sets last for several years but can warp, stain or crack, and the markings can wear. One-piece steel like the Spring Chef avoids loosening handles. Replace any cup that has a bent rim, because it will no longer level accurately.
